clinicalPearls: Transient synovitis is the commonest cause of acute atraumatic hip pain and limp in young children, typically affecting the pre-school and early school-age group, and is more common in boys.
A preceding or concurrent viral upper respiratory tract illness is frequently reported, supporting a post-infectious reactive aetiology.
Affected children are usually well or only mildly unwell, afebrile or with low-grade temperature, and tend to limp or remain weight-bearing rather than refuse to move the limb entirely.
The hip is characteristically held flexed, abducted and externally rotated, with pain and guarding most marked at the extremes of internal rotation.
The central clinical task is to distinguish it from septic arthritis; validated prediction rules combining weight-bearing status, fever and inflammatory markers help stratify risk.
Inflammatory markers and the white cell count are normal or only mildly raised, in contrast to the marked elevation typical of septic arthritis.
Ultrasound commonly demonstrates a hip joint effusion but cannot reliably differentiate a sterile from an infected collection.
It remains a diagnosis of exclusion; management is supportive with rest and simple analgesia or anti-inflammatory agents, with planned review to confirm resolution.
reference.pathophysiology: Transient synovitis is a self-limiting, non-pyogenic inflammation of the hip synovium that produces a sterile reactive effusion and consequent joint irritability. It is widely regarded as a post-infectious or reactive phenomenon, frequently following a viral illness, in which transient immune-mediated synovial inflammation and effusion raise intra-articular pressure and provoke pain, guarding and a characteristic protective posture. The synovial reaction resolves spontaneously without cartilage destruction, distinguishing it fundamentally from the pyogenic, cartilage-damaging process of septic arthritis with which it is most often confused.
additionalDifferentials: Osteomyelitis of the proximal femur or pelvis
Slipped capital femoral epiphysis, particularly in older or heavier children
Reactive or post-streptococcal arthritis and acute rheumatic fever
Occult trauma or malignancy such as leukaemia presenting with bone or joint pain
additionalInvestigations: Hip ultrasound to detect and quantify effusion and to guide aspiration where needed
CRP, ESR and full blood count
Blood cultures where infection is suspected
Plain radiographs of the pelvis and hips, including anteroposterior and frog-lateral views, to exclude Perthes, slipped epiphysis and fracture
Joint aspiration with Gram stain, culture and cell count when septic arthritis cannot be excluded
MRI where osteomyelitis, Perthes disease or occult pathology is considered
Peripheral blood film and further haematological work-up if atypical or systemic features are present
redFlags: Inability to bear weight combined with fever and markedly raised inflammatory markers, suggesting septic arthritis
Systemic toxicity, rigors or a rapidly deteriorating child
Night pain, weight loss, bruising or pallor suggesting malignancy
Symptoms failing to settle within the expected short timeframe
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent and the condition is self-limiting, with most children recovering fully within one to two weeks; a minority experience recurrent episodes. Rarely, a small proportion of children initially labelled as having transient synovitis are subsequently diagnosed with Perthes disease.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing early septic arthritis as transient synovitis and delaying intervention
Relying on ultrasound to differentiate a sterile from a septic effusion
Missing Perthes disease or a slipped epiphysis on inadequate radiographs that omit frog-lateral views
Failing to safety-net and arrange review for non-resolving symptoms
Overlooking leukaemia presenting as bone or joint pain
references: Kocher criteria for differentiating septic arthritis from transient synovitis of the hip
management: Rest, activity limitation and simple analgesia or a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug for symptomatic relief, as the synovitis is self-limiting

Actively exclude septic arthritis using validated prediction rules combining weight-bearing status, fever and inflammatory markers, with hip ultrasound and joint aspiration where infection cannot be ruled out
Reassurance with outpatient management for the well, afebrile, weight-bearing child
Clear safety-netting to re-present with fever, increasing pain or refusal to weight-bear, prompting re-evaluation for septic arthritis
Clinical follow-up to confirm resolution within one to two weeks and to detect the minority who later declare Perthes disease
Refer to paediatric orthopaedics when the diagnosis is uncertain, symptoms persist, or septic arthritis is suspected
